claim: RasGRP1 and SOS are Ras-specific nucleotide exchange factors that have distinct roles in lymphocyte development.
source: RasGRP1 and SOS are Ras-specific nucleotide exchange factors that have distinct roles in lymphocyte development.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Dower et al., 2000; Ebinu et al., 2000; Kortum et al., 2011) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: RasGRP1 is important in some cancers and autoimmune diseases.
source: RasGRP1 is important in some cancers and autoimmune diseases but, in contrast to SOS, its regulatory mechanisms are poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the manuscript discussing RasGRP1's role in various diseases.

claim: The regulatory mechanisms of RasGRP1 are poorly understood in contrast to SOS.
source: RasGRP1 is important in some cancers and autoimmune diseases but, in contrast to SOS, its regulatory mechanisms are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: A crystal structure of a fragment of RasGRP1 shows the Ras-binding site is blocked by an interdomain linker.
source: We present a crystal structure of a fragment of RasGRP1 in which the Ras-binding site is blocked by an interdomain linker and the membrane-interaction surface of RasGRP1 is hidden within a dimerization interface that may be stabilized by the C-terminal oligomerization domain.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2, Table 1).

claim: The membrane-interaction surface of RasGRP1 is hidden within a dimerization interface.
source: We present a crystal structure of a fragment of RasGRP1 in which the Ras-binding site is blocked by an interdomain linker and the membrane-interaction surface of RasGRP1 is hidden within a dimerization interface that may be stabilized by the C-terminal oligomerization domain.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing C1 domain dimerization (Figure 2B, Figure 6).

claim: The dimerization interface may be stabilized by the C-terminal oligomerization domain.
source: We present a crystal structure of a fragment of RasGRP1 in which the Ras-binding site is blocked by an interdomain linker and the membrane-interaction surface of RasGRP1 is hidden within a dimerization interface that may be stabilized by the C-terminal oligomerization domain.
evidence: This is speculative based on the coiled coil structure (Figure 4) and its potential role in stabilizing the dimer.

claim: Calcium binding to the regulatory module generates substantial conformational changes incompatible with the inactive assembly.
source: NMR data demonstrate that calcium binding to the regulatory module generates substantial conformational changes that are incompatible with the inactive assembly.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data comparing apo and calcium-bound states (Figure 10—figure supplement 2, Figure 10—figure supplement 5).

claim: RasGRP1 can be maintained in an inactive state that is poised for activation by calcium and membrane-localization signals.
source: These features allow RasGRP1 to be maintained in an inactive state that is poised for activation by calcium and membrane-localization signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ras cycles between an inactive GDP-bound form and an active GTP-bound form.
source: Ras cycles between an inactive GDP-bound form and an active GTP-bound form, and in both states the nucleotide is very tightly bound (Vetter and Wittinghofer, 2001; Rajalingam et al., 2007; Ahearn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors loosen the grip of Ras on the bound nucleotide, allowing GTP loading and activation.
source: A critical regulatory function is therefore provided by the action of guanine nucleotide exchange factors, which loosen the grip of Ras on the bound nucleotide, allowing GTP loading and activation (Bos et al., 2007; Cherfils and Zeghouf, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RasGRP proteins have tissue-specific expression patterns.
source: The RasGRP and Ras guanine nucleotide releasing factor (RasGRF) families of exchange factors have tissue-specific expression patterns whereas SOS proteins are expressed ubiquitously (Stone, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stone, 2011.

claim: SOS proteins are expressed ubiquitously.
source: The RasGRP and Ras guanine nucleotide releasing factor (RasGRF) families of exchange factors have tissue-specific expression patterns whereas SOS proteins are expressed ubiquitously (Stone, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stone, 2011.

claim: RasGRP proteins activate Ras in a manner that is non-redundant with SOS.
source: RasGRP proteins have been studied most extensively in T and B lymphocytes (Aiba et al., 2004; Brodie et al., 2004; Coughlin et al., 2005; Roose et al., 2005; Limnander et al., 2011) where they activate Ras in a manner that is non-redundant with SOS (Dower et al., 2000; Roose et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: RasGRP proteins play important roles in squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma.
source: In addition, RasGRP proteins play important roles in squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma (Luke et al., 2007; Oki-Idouchi and Lorenzo, 2007; Diez et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2011), T cell- and myeloid- leukemia (Reuther et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Klinger et al., 2005; Lauchle et al., 2009; Oki et al., 2012; Hartzell et al., 2013) and prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010) that are distinct from those of SOS.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: RasGRP proteins play important roles in T cell- and myeloid-leukemia.
source: In addition, RasGRP proteins play important roles in squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma (Luke et al., 2007; Oki-Idouchi and Lorenzo, 2007; Diez et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2011), T cell- and myeloid- leukemia (Reuther et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Klinger et al., 2005; Lauchle et al., 2009; Oki et al., 2012; Hartzell et al., 2013) and prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010) that are distinct from those of SOS.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: RasGRP proteins play important roles in prostate cancer.
source: In addition, RasGRP proteins play important roles in squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma (Luke et al., 2007; Oki-Idouchi and Lorenzo, 2007; Diez et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2011), T cell- and myeloid- leukemia (Reuther et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Klinger et al., 2005; Lauchle et al., 2009; Oki et al., 2012; Hartzell et al., 2013) and prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010) that are distinct from those of SOS.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: Ras signaling plays a critical role in T lymphocyte development.
source: Developing T lymphocytes pass through quality control checkpoints to generate a repertoire of protective but self-tolerant immune cells (Starr et al., 2003) and Ras signaling plays a critical role in this progression (Swan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Both RasGRP1 and SOS are recruited to the membrane in response to T cell receptor stimulation during T lymphocyte development.
source: In response to T cell receptor stimulation during T lymphocyte development, both RasGRP1 and SOS are recruited to the membrane where they encounter membrane-anchored Ras.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The requirements for RasGRP1 and SOS during different T lymphocyte checkpoints are distinct.
source: Interestingly, knockout mouse models have revealed that the requirements for RasGRP1 and SOS during different T lymphocyte checkpoints are distinct, despite the fact that they both convert Ras•GDP to Ras•GTP (Dower et al., 2000; Layer et al., 2003; Kortum et al., 2011, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to knockout mouse studies.

claim: Elevated RasGRP1 mRNA expression has been reported in T cell leukemia microarray studies.
source: Elevated RasGRP1 mRNA expression has been reported in T cell leukemia microarray studies and is found frequently in pediatric T cell leukemia in which it stimulates the growth of this blood cancer (Oki et al., 2012; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to microarray studies.

claim: Elevated RasGRP1 expression stimulates the growth of pediatric T cell leukemia.
source: Elevated RasGRP1 mRNA expression has been reported in T cell leukemia microarray studies and is found frequently in pediatric T cell leukemia in which it stimulates the growth of this blood cancer (Oki et al., 2012; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on pediatric T cell leukemia.

claim: Reduced RasGRP1 expression has been reported for autoimmune patients with lupus erythematosus.
source: Conversely, reduced RasGRP1 expression has been reported for autoimmune patients with lupus erythematosus where it may play a role in aberrant DNA methylation in T cells (Yasuda et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on lupus patients.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in RasGRP1 have been described in genome-wide association studies of autoimmune diabetes and thyroid disease.
source: Additionally, single nucleotide polymorphisms in RasGRP1 have been described in genome-wide association studies of autoimmune diabetes and thyroid disease (Qu et al., 2009; Plagnol et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome-wide association studies.

claim: The Ras-specific exchange factors have similar catalytic modules that contain two domains.
source: The Ras-specific exchange factors have similar catalytic modules that contain two domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by structural comparisons in the manuscript.

claim: The Cdc25 domain interacts directly with Ras and dislodges the bound nucleotide.
source: The Cdc25 domain interacts directly with Ras and dislodges the bound nucleotide (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: The REM domain is usually essential for activity but its function does not appear to be conserved in different exchange factors.
source: The Ras exchanger motif (REM) domain that is associated with the Cdc25 domain is usually essential for activity but its function does not appear to be conserved in different exchange factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional comparisons across exchange factor families.

claim: Each family of Ras-specific exchange factors contains distinct regulatory domains that enable Ras signaling to be activated in response to a variety of upstream receptor stimuli.
source: Each family of Ras-specific exchange factors contains distinct regulatory domains that enable Ras signaling to be activated in response to a variety of upstream receptor stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Understanding of how regulatory domains control activation is limited to SOS and Epac2.
source: Despite the importance of the regulatory domains for controlling activation, our understanding of how these work at the structural level is limited to SOS (Sondermann et al., 2004; Gureasko et al., 2008, 2010) and the Rap-specific exchange factor, Epac2 (Rehmann et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies on SOS and Epac2.

claim: RasGRP1 primes SOS for activation by generating an initial burst of Ras•GTP.
source: One important role for RasGRP1 is to prime SOS for activation by generating an initial burst of Ras•GTP (Roose et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roose et al., 2007.

claim: Ras•GTP activates SOS by binding to an allosteric site that bridges the REM and Cdc25 domains.
source: This priming function of RasGRP1 potentiates SOS activity because of a feedback loop in which Ras•GTP activates SOS by binding to an allosteric site that bridges the REM and Cdc25 domains (Margarit et al., 2003; Boykevisch et al., 2006; Sondermann et al., 2004; Gureasko et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies on SOS.

claim: Ras•GTP binding to the allosteric site helps stabilize SOS at the plasma membrane.
source: Ras•GTP binding to the allosteric site helps stabilize SOS at the plasma membrane and promotes the conversion of Ras•GDP to Ras•GTP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on SOS mechanism.

claim: The action of RasGRP1 in initiating the positive feedback loop of SOS leads to ultrasensitive ERK activation in Jurkat T cells.
source: The action of RasGRP1 in initiating the positive feedback loop of SOS leads to ultrasensitive ERK activation in Jurkat T cells and has been postulated to define the sharp boundary between positively and negatively selecting ligands during thymocyte development (Das et al., 2009; Prasad et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ERK activation.

claim: The catalytic module of RasGRP1 is followed by an EF domain with a predicted pair of EF hands.
source: The catalytic module of RasGRP1 is followed by an EF domain with a predicted pair of EF hands (EF1 and EF2 modules), a diacylglycerol-binding C1 domain, and a C-terminal segment that includes a primarily unstructured region of ∼140 residues and a predicted coiled coil (Ebinu et al., 1998; Beaulieu et al., 2007; Zahedi et al., 2011) (see Figure 1B for the domain architecture of RasGRP1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and predictions, supported by citations.

claim: A portion of the C-terminal segment of RasGRP1 enhances membrane recruitment through electrostatic interactions with phosphoinositides.
source: A portion of the C-terminal segment of RasGRP1 has been demonstrated to enhance membrane recruitment through electrostatic interactions with phosphoinositides (Zahedi et al., 2011), and the physiological importance of this segment is illustrated by impaired T lymphocyte development in mice lacking this part of the protein (Fuller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Addition of a membrane localization tag to a fragment of RasGRP1 does not lead to constitutive Ras activation.
source: However, addition of a membrane localization tag to a fragment of RasGRP1 does not lead to constitutive Ras activation, suggesting more complexity in the regulatory mechanisms (Beaulieu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Beaulieu et al., 2007.

claim: There are conflicting reports as to whether calcium binding to the EF domain is coupled to the localization and activity of RasGRP1.
source: The presence of two EF hands suggests that they might be responsible for the sensitivity of RasGRP1 to calcium, but there are conflicting reports as to whether calcium binding to the EF domain is coupled to the localization and activity of RasGRP1 (Ebinu et al., 1998; Lorenzo et al., 2000; Tazmini et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies with conflicting results.

claim: Two crystal structures of RasGRP1 span the folded domains of the protein and omit predicted intrinsically disordered segments.
source: To identify the structural basis for the regulation of RasGRP1, we have determined two crystal structures of RasGRP1. Together, these structures span the folded domains of the protein and omit the N-terminal 50 residue segment and the ∼140 residue segment immediately following the C1 domain that are both predicted to be intrinsically disordered.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript (Tables 1 and 2, Figures 2 and 4).

claim: The first structure includes the REM, Cdc25, EF and C1 domains and suggests a structural basis for autoinhibition by the regulatory domains.
source: The first structure includes the REM, Cdc25, EF and C1 domains and suggests a structural basis for autoinhibition by the regulatory domains.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data (Figure 2, Table 1).

claim: Key aspects of the autoinhibition mechanisms involve occlusion of the Ras-binding site by an interdomain linker.
source: Key aspects of the mechanisms we identify involve occlusion of the Ras-binding site by an interdomain linker and dimerization-mediated masking of the C1 domains.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing the linker blocking the Ras-binding site (Figure 5).

claim: Key aspects of the autoinhibition mechanisms involve dimerization-mediated masking of the C1 domains.
source: Key aspects of the mechanisms we identify involve occlusion of the Ras-binding site by an interdomain linker and dimerization-mediated masking of the C1 domains.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing C1 domain dimerization (Figure 6).

claim: The second structure shows that the C-terminal segment forms a parallel coiled coil that facilitates dimerization.
source: The second structure is pertinent in this regard, as it shows that the C-terminal segment forms a parallel coiled coil that facilitates dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of RasGRP1CC (Figure 4, Table 2).

claim: The EF domain has a single Ca2+ binding site.
source: The EF domain, which we demonstrate has a single Ca2+ binding site, is likely to contribute to activation through a calcium-triggered conformational change that we have analyzed using NMR.
evidence: This is supported by ITC and NMR data (Figure 10, Table 3).

claim: The EF domain is likely to contribute to activation through a calcium-triggered conformational change.
source: The EF domain, which we demonstrate has a single Ca2+ binding site, is likely to contribute to activation through a calcium-triggered conformational change that we have analyzed using NMR.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data showing conformational changes upon calcium binding (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).

claim: Membrane docking and calcium binding drive RasGRP1 activation by disrupting the C1 interface and removing an inhibitory linker that blocks the Ras-binding site.
source: Our results are consistent with a mechanism wherein membrane docking and calcium binding drive RasGRP1 activation by disrupting the C1 interface and removing an inhibitory linker that blocks the Ras-binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A crystal structure of RasGRP1CEC was determined at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: We determined a crystal structure of RasGRP1CEC at 3.0 Å resolution (Table 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The catalytic modules of RasGRP1 and SOS are structurally similar.
source: The catalytic modules of RasGRP1 and SOS are structurally similar.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3.

claim: The structures of the regulatory domains and their inhibitory interactions with the catalytic module are different in RasGRP1 and SOS.
source: In contrast, the structures of the regulatory domains and their inhibitory interactions with the catalytic module are different in RasGRP1 and SOS.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Cdc25 domain consists of a compact bundle of 10 helices that forms the core of the structure.
source: The Cdc25 domain consists of a compact bundle of 10 helices that forms the core of the structure.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2).

claim: Two antiparallel and tightly packed helices form a prominent hairpin that protrudes from the Cdc25 core.
source: Two antiparallel and tightly packed helices that form a prominent hairpin protrude from this core.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2).

claim: The helical hairpin of the Cdc25 domain splays the switch 1 segment of Ras away from the rest of the protein, thereby removing the nucleotide.
source: The structure of nucleotide-free Ras bound to the SOS Cdc25 domain showed that the switch 2 region of Ras docks on the helical bundle of the Cdc25 domain, and that the helical hairpin splays the switch 1 segment of Ras away from the rest of the protein, thereby removing the nucleotide (Figure 3A) (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998; Margarit et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies on SOS-Ras complexes.

claim: Empty Ras is expected to bind the Cdc25 domain of RasGRP1 in a manner similar to that observed for Ras binding to SOS.
source: Based on the close structural similarity of the Cdc25 domains, empty Ras is expected to bind the Cdc25 domain of RasGRP1 in a manner similar to that observed for Ras binding to SOS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity between RasGRP1 and SOS Cdc25 domains.

claim: The hydrophobic properties of residues in SOS that interact with Tyr 64 and the switch 2 element of Ras are conserved in RasGRP1.
source: The hydrophobic properties of residues in SOS that form a pocket at the base of the helical hairpin and interact with Tyr 64 and the switch 2 element of Ras (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998) are conserved in RasGRP1.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural comparison.

claim: The REM domain of RasGRP1 interacts with the helical hairpin of the Cdc25 domain in a manner similar to that seen in SOS.
source: The REM domain of RasGRP1 interacts with the helical hairpin of the Cdc25 domain in a manner similar to that seen in SOS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and compared to SOS (Figure 3).

claim: The folds of the REM domains of RasGRP1 and SOS are similar with the exception of a helical extension in SOS that is absent in RasGRP1.
source: Despite the limited sequence identity between the REM domains of RasGRP1 and SOS, the folds are similar with the exception of a helical extension in SOS that is absent in RasGRP1.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison (Figure 3).

claim: The REM domain extension in SOS helps orient the N-terminal regulatory module, which occludes the allosteric Ras-binding site in the autoinhibited state.
source: The REM domain extension in SOS helps orient the N-terminal regulatory module (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for SOS domain architecture), which occludes the allosteric Ras-binding site in the autoinhibited state (Sondermann et al., 2004; Gureasko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies on SOS.

claim: In the absence of Ras•GTP at the allosteric site, the helical hairpin of SOS adopts a closed conformation that partially occludes the Ras binding site.
source: In the absence of Ras•GTP at the allosteric site, the helical hairpin of SOS adopts a closed conformation that partially occludes the Ras binding site.
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies on SOS.

claim: A ~10° rotation of the SOS helical hairpin is necessary to achieve a conformation competent for Ras binding to the active site.
source: A ∼10° rotation of the SOS helical hairpin is necessary to achieve a conformation competent for Ras binding to the active site.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of SOS in different states.

claim: The RasGRP1 helical hairpin in the absence of Ras is rotated ~15° away from the active site with respect to its orientation in active SOS, consistent with an open conformation poised to bind to Ras.
source: In contrast, the RasGRP1 helical hairpin (residues 355–398) in the absence of Ras is rotated ∼15° away from the active site with respect to its orientation in active SOS, which is consistent with an open conformation that is poised to bind to Ras (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RasGRP1 regulation may not rely on allosteric control using the REM domain.
source: This critical difference in the helical hairpin orientation implies that RasGRP1 regulation may not rely on allosteric control using the REM domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural differences between RasGRP1 and SOS.

claim: The helical hairpin conformation for RasGRP1 is similar to the orientation observed for the isolated Cdc25 domain of RasGRF.
source: The helical hairpin conformation for RasGRP1 is similar to the orientation observed for the isolated Cdc25 domain of RasGRF (Freedman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study on RasGRF.

claim: For Epac2, the helical hairpin is in an open conformation in the absence of Rap.
source: For Epac2, the helical hairpin is in an open conformation in the absence of Rap (Rehmann et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies on Epac2.

claim: The regulatory module of RasGRP1, containing the EF and C1 domains, interacts extensively with the Cdc25 domain.
source: The regulatory module of RasGRP1, containing the EF and C1 domains, interacts extensively with the Cdc25 domain.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2).

claim: In SOS, the regulatory domains are organized around the REM domain, making no contact with the Cdc25 domain.
source: This is in contrast to the situation with SOS, where a different set of regulatory domains is organized around the REM domain, making no contact with the Cdc25 domain.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of SOS.

claim: The EF domain in RasGRP1 interacts with one side of the Cdc25 domain, adjacent to the catalytic Ras-binding site.
source: The EF domain in RasGRP1 interacts with one side of the Cdc25 domain, adjacent to the catalytic Ras-binding site, with the C1 domain extending from the opposite side of the EF domain.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2).

claim: Metal ions are not present in either EF hand in the crystal structure.
source: Metal ions are not present in either EF hand in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The second of the two EF hands is structurally degenerate in that one of the two helices present in canonical EF hands is missing and is replaced by a loop.
source: The second of the two EF hands is structurally degenerate in that one of the two helices present in canonical EF hands is missing and is replaced by a loop that we refer to as the EF2 connector.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 9).

claim: The RasGRP1 C1 domain is structurally similar to other C1 domains, with a Cα rmsd of 0.4 Å over 52 aligned Cα atoms when compared with the C1 domain of PKCδ.
source: The RasGRP1 C1 domain is structurally similar to other C1 domains, with a Cα rmsd of 0.4 Å over 52 aligned Cα atoms when compared with the C1 domain of PKCδ (Zhang et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with PKCδ C1 domain.

claim: The C1 domain docks onto a small region of the EF domain using the surface distal from the membrane-interacting residues.
source: The C1 domain docks onto a small region of the EF domain using the surface distal from the membrane-interacting residues.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2).

claim: An extensive dimer interface is generated at a twofold symmetry axis in the crystal, burying ~2500 Å2 of surface area between the two subunits in the dimer.
source: An extensive dimer interface is generated at a twofold symmetry axis in the crystal, burying ∼2500 Å2 of surface area between the two subunits in the dimer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The C1 domain from one subunit in the dimer interacts with the Cdc25, EF and C1 domains of the other subunit.
source: The C1 domain from one subunit in the dimer interacts with the Cdc25, EF and C1 domains of the other subunit.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 2B).

claim: Residues 747–789 within the C-terminal region of RasGRP1 are predicted to contain a coiled coil.
source: Residues 747–789 within the C-terminal region are predicted by the COILS webserver (Lupas et al., 1991) to contain a coiled coil and are spanned by the RasGRP1CC construct.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using the COILS webserver.

claim: The crystal structure of RasGRP1CC was determined at 1.6 Å resolution.
source: We determined the crystal structure of RasGRP1CC at 1.6 Å resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystallographic data in Table 2.

claim: Two molecules in the asymmetric unit of the RasGRP1CC crystal form a parallel, dimeric coiled coil of nearly 10 helical turns.
source: Two molecules in the asymmetric unit of the crystal form a parallel, dimeric coiled coil of nearly 10 helical turns that is structurally similar to canonical coiled coil proteins such as GCN4 (O'Shea et al., 1991) (Figure 4A, Table 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 4A, Table 2).

claim: Leucine and isoleucine residues stabilize the RasGRP1CC dimer.
source: Leucine and isoleucine residues stabilize the dimer, and a pair of glutamine residues in the core maintains the proper sequence register between the two helices.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 4A).

claim: Two pairs of ionic interactions (Glu 754-Lys 759′ and Glu 782-Lys 783′) further stabilize the RasGRP1CC dimer.
source: Two pairs of ionic interactions (Glu 754-Lys 759′ and Glu 782-Lys 783′, where the primes refer to the second subunit in the dimer) further stabilize the dimer.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 4A).

claim: An electron density map reveals additional electron density for a peptide traversing the Ras binding site in the Cdc25 domain.
source: An electron density map calculated with phases derived from the model for the four domains of RasGRP1CEC reveals additional electron density for a peptide traversing the Ras binding site in the Cdc25 domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density map (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The electron density can be assigned unambiguously to a portion of the linker between the Cdc25 and EF domains.
source: This electron density can be assigned unambiguously to a portion of the linker between the Cdc25 and EF domains, but strong electron density is present only for the central eight residues of the linker.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the electron density map.

claim: Several residues in the visible portion of the Cdc25-EF linker, including Val 450, Val 452 and Trp 454, dock within a hydrophobic groove at the base of the RasGRP1 helical hairpin.
source: The visible portion of the linker shows that several residues, including Val 450, Val 452 and Trp 454, dock within a hydrophobic groove at the base of the RasGRP1 helical hairpin (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (Figure 5A).

claim: The hydrophobic groove at the base of the RasGRP1 helical hairpin is the expected binding site for the switch 2 segment of Ras, including Tyr 64.
source: This groove is the expected binding site for the switch 2 segment of Ras, including Tyr 64, which is absolutely required for recognition of Ras by SOS (Hall et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with SOS-Ras structures and supported by citation.

claim: Occupation of the hydrophobic groove by the Cdc25-EF linker will prevent Ras binding and nucleotide exchange.
source: Clearly, occupation of this site on the Cdc25 domain by the Cdc25-EF linker will prevent Ras binding and nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the structural observation.

claim: Trp 454 and the hydrophobic nature of the Cdc25-EF linker region are highly conserved in all RasGRP family proteins.
source: Trp 454 and the hydrophobic nature of this region of the linker are highly conserved in all RasGRP family proteins, including those in distantly related organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutation of Trp 454 and other conserved linker residues leads to a ~2.5-fold increase in RasGRP1CEC activity towards soluble Ras in vitro.
source: Mutation of Trp 454 and other conserved linker residues leads to a ∼2.5-fold increase in RasGRP1CEC activity towards soluble Ras in vitro (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro nucleotide exchange assay (Figure 5C).

claim: Mutations in the Cdc25-EF linker have minimal effect in a construct lacking the EF and C1 domains.
source: Mutations in the linker have minimal effect in a construct lacking the EF and C1 domains (data not shown), presumably because the loss of the C-terminal tether of the Cdc25-EF linker results in increased flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on unpublished data.

claim: RasGRP1CEC is ~3.5-fold less active than the isolated catalytic module (RasGRPcat) towards Ras in solution.
source: Consistent with this idea, RasGRP1CEC is ∼3.5-fold less active than the isolated catalytic module (REM + Cdc25, RasGRPcat) towards Ras in solution (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly measured in the in vitro nucleotide exchange assay (Figure 5C).

claim: Mutation of Asp 453 and Trp 454 in the Cdc25-EF linker increased ERK phosphorylation 1.7 to 2.3-fold in cells.
source: Using this assay, we found that mutation of Asp 453 and Trp 454 in the Cdc25-EF linker increased ERK phosphorylation 1.7 to 2.3-fold, over the entire range of RasGRP1 protein expression levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly measured in the FACS-based cell assay (Figure 5D).

claim: Mutation of Trp 454 and two or four other residues in the Cdc25-EF linker led to an additional increase in P-ERK levels.
source: Mutation of Trp 454 and two or four other residues in the Cdc25-EF linker led to an additional increase in P-ERK levels.
evidence: This is directly measured in the FACS-based cell assay (Figure 5D).

claim: The Cdc25-EF linker plays an inhibitory role in full-length RasGRP1.
source: These results confirm that the Cdc25-EF linker plays an inhibitory role in full-length RasGRP1.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis experiments in cells (Figure 5D).

claim: The C1 domain of RasGRP1 structurally resembles that of PKCδ, which is shown bound to a diacylglycerol mimic.
